# 3. An autogenerated certificate label ends with a digest of the id

Date: 2026-11-02. Status: accepted. Relates to GitHub issue #118 and
`docs/design/muxcon.md` section 2 (handshake and TLS trust).

## Context

Both autogenerated TLS certificates — the MuxCon listener's and the web console's — put `server.id` in
their X.509 CommonName. RFC 5280 caps that attribute at 64 characters and `cryptography` refuses to build
a certificate past it. A node with a longer id therefore logged `TLS autogen failed`, refused to fall back
to plaintext, and ran on with no federation listener at all (issue #118, fixed in `86aaf34`).

That fix cut the id at 64 characters. It left a second problem, which `MXC-05` walks past daily: two nodes
whose ids share a 64-character prefix carry the same CommonName. Before this ADR, `openmux/common/identity.py`
was measured on two ids of 87 and 89 characters, equal up to position 64. Both produced one identical
64-character label.

Nothing reads the CommonName today. The two builders in `openmux/server/adapters/muxcon.py` and
`openmux/server/web_console.py` write it, and no code reads it back. Link trust rides on the certificate
fingerprint, which the initiator pins on first connect (`tls_tofu`) and compares on every later connect.
The collision therefore breaks no link.

It is still a decision, not a detail. The next surface that shows a certificate — a peer list, viewer
guidance, or a CA-signed mode — inherits whichever rule the label carries. At that point a label cannot be
both "the node's id" and 64 characters long while two nodes claim it, and the person comparing them has no
way to tell which is wrong.

## Decision

Keep the ceiling. Shorten by digest, not by cut. `certificate_cn()` in `openmux/common/identity.py`
returns:

- the id unchanged when it fits within 64 characters, so no normal node sees a difference;
- otherwise the first 50 characters of the id, the ASCII mark `..`, and the first 12 hex digits of the
  SHA-256 of the whole id.

The two labels below are the real output for the two ids quoted in the Context section:

```text
openmux-site-a-rack-00112233445566778899aabbccddee..b7a28b6bbf55   (-hub-primary-01)
openmux-site-a-rack-00112233445566778899aabbccddee..2f585a91a72e   (-hub-secondary-02)
```

Three rules follow from that:

1. The digest covers the whole id, so a difference past position 64 changes the label. A plain cut hides it.
2. Twelve hex digits is 48 bits. Two colliding labels then need an engineered SHA-256 prefix, not a shared
   site or rack name. That is enough for a label no code trusts.
3. The head stays 50 characters, which is long enough to read the machine out of. Trimming it to make the
   digest longer would trade the only job the label has for a margin that job does not need.

Keep one rule for both certificates: the MuxCon builder and the web console builder call `certificate_cn()`,
the module whose header already owns the server identity on every surface. A third builder must call it too,
rather than invent a second shortening rule.

Report the condition once per config load. `warn_long_server_id()` in the same module logs one WARNING naming the
identity, its length, the ceiling, and the label a certificate gets. `OpenMuxServer._reload_config_from_disk()`
calls it, so the WARNING appears at startup and on every reload — SIGHUP, SIGUSR1, or a Config Editor action — and
it does not depend on TLS being enabled. Reporting the length only where a certificate is BUILT hides the condition
from an operator who has not enabled MuxCon yet, which is the moment the fix is cheapest. One shared sentence,
because two TLS surfaces that describe one condition in two different words read like two different problems.

## Consequences

- A node that generates a new certificate after this change gets a different label for a long id. Both
  builders reuse a `server.crt` that already exists, so a deployed node keeps its certificate, keeps its
  fingerprint, and makes no peer re-pin anything. Only a fresh install or a deleted TLS directory changes
  what a viewer shows.
- The WARNING fires from the config load, so an operator sees it whether or not a certificate exists yet. The
  reporter runs once per load, because `_reload_config_from_disk()` runs per load and per deliberate reload and
  never on a timer, so the log keeps one line per load instead of repeating the same length forever.
- A certificate generated while the cut rule was in force keeps its cut label, so two prefix-sharing nodes
  deployed in that window still read alike until their certificates are rebuilt.
  Rebuilding is not free — a new certificate means a new fingerprint, and an initiator with `tls_tofu: true`
  rejects the node until its entry in `<state dir>/muxcon/known_peers.yaml` is dropped on the dialling side.
  Rotate only when the key itself needs it, not to improve a label.
- `CHANGELOG.md` (1.0.5) tells an operator who compares a CommonName against a long `server.id` that the
  label now ends in `..` plus a digest instead of stopping mid-id.
- `tests/test_server_identity.py` pins the rule at the resolver: an id at the ceiling is untouched, a longer
  id stays inside it, two ids sharing a 64-character prefix differ, the answer is never empty, and the reporter
  names a long identity while staying silent on one a certificate can carry.
- `tests/server/test_main_coverage.py` pins the WARNING to the load path: a long `server.id` reports once while the
  server is built and again on reload, and a short one stays quiet in both.
- `tests/test_muxcon_adapter_basic.py` pins it through the real builder, so the rule cannot drift from what
  a certificate actually carries. `MXC-05` and `MXC-06` keep proving over a live pinned link that a long id still
  gets a working TLS listener.
- `tests/test_web_console_tls_autogen.py` covers the console builder, which had no test at all before this change:
  its CommonName stays inside the ceiling for a long `server.id`.
- A surface that needs the id must read `server.id` or carry it in a certificate extension. It must not
  parse the label: the head is display text, and the digest is not reversible.
- Issue #118 also records that a node whose federation listener never started still reported itself healthy.
  This ADR does not settle that. A refused listener is a gap the server must report, and it belongs to
  issue #107 ("listener not built or bound"), not to the label.
